title: Capacity-affinity credits and graceful cross-region throttling
creator: Aisha Kapoor
description: Problem statement: Requests to Redwood-hosted models experience uneven latency and tail spikes when traffic shifts between regions or when an edge region temporarily loses capacity. Existing solutions either perform hard failover (fast but disruptive) or simple latency hedging (less disruptive but expensive). We need a policy that preserves locality and SLOs while providing graceful degradation when capacity constraints occur, minimizing user-visible errors and token-cost blowups.
goals: 1) Keep >=99.9% p95 latency SLO for high-tier customers by preferring local regions when healthy. 2) Limit cross-region egress and cold-starts to avoid cost/latency regressions. 3) Provide deterministic, observable behavior when regions become constrained: soft throttling, credit-driven pin eviction, and controlled failover. 4) Integrate with circuit breakers/capacity signals and Console dashboards.
success_criteria: 1) New policy maintains p95 latency <= SLO in chaos test across 3 regions for 95% of runs. 2) Cross-region egress increase <= 10% under typical load bursts. 3) No customer-facing 5xx increases beyond 0.05% during failover windows. 4) On-call runbook reduces mean restore time by enabling automated credit-based reroute decisions.
proposal: Introduce a Capacity-Affinity Credits policy: each region allocates per-customer affinity credits based on historical locality and current capacity. Credits represent short-term routing preference. When a request arrives, the router computes a score = latency_score * affinity_credit_multiplier * capacity_factor. The router prefers endpoints with highest score. If capacity signals dip below thresholds, we trigger soft circuit breaker modes: (a) Slow-path degrade: reduce max-concurrency and enable prefix caching for that customer. (b) Credit drain: begin consuming affinity credits to steer traffic away gradually. (c) Controlled failover: once credits exhausted and capacity still low, incrementally shift a window of requests to secondary regions using hedged requests with progressively larger timeouts.
design_decisions: 1) Use existing region capacity probes (Agent-probe) as capacity_factor input; smooth with exponential moving average over 30s. 2) Affinity credits are per-customer, bucketed by route and model family. Credits refill at a tunable rate (default 5 credits/min). 3) Latency_score uses normalized recent p95 latency (lower latency => higher score). 4) Circuit breaker has three states: CLOSED (normal), SOFT_OPEN (rate-limited, prioritizes cached or low-cost variants), OPEN (reject or fast-fail with fallback model). 5) All decisions are deterministic and logged with decision_reason tags for traceability.
rollout_plan: Phase 0: Simulation using traffic replay + offline scoring (2 weeks). Phase 1: Canary in us-west-2 for internal tenants (1 week). Phase 2: Limited customer rollout (5% of production) with observability flags (2 weeks). Phase 3: Gradual ramp to global by region pairs (4 weeks). Each phase gated by SLO metrics and credit burn rate limits.
monitoring: Dashboards to add: per-customer affinity credit balance over time, per-region capacity factor, routing decision distribution, cross-region egress delta, soft-circuit-breaker activation rate, and customer p95 before/after reroute. Alerting: high credit burn rate (>50% of budget/min sustained 2 min), sustained capacity_factor <0.4 for >30s, cross-region egress increase >15% above baseline.
dependencies: PM-412: rollout gating and customer selection
risks: Mis-tuned credit refill leads to oscillation between regions.
Affordability risk: too many hedged requests increasing token costs.
Edge-case: small customers with limited historical locality may be over-evicted.
Observability gaps could make debugging routing-driven regressions slow.
mitigations: Start with conservative credit drain rates, require manual approval to increase hedging window, implement emergency kill-switch per customer/region in Console, and add synthetic tests exercising credit exhaustion scenarios.
testing_plan: 1) Unit tests for scoring and state transitions. 2) Integration test: two-region cluster simulation with controllable capacity injection and traffic replay. 3) Chaos test: induce capacity drops and verify soft-open behavior. 4) Cost analysis: simulate hedging rates and project token egress delta.
rollout_kpis: p95 latency by customer tier, percentage of requests routed cross-region, affinity credit equilibrium (avg credits/customer), hedged-request ratio, token cost delta per 100k requests.
notes: This design tries to trade small, predictable cross-region traffic for stable latency SLOs instead of large-scale bulk failovers. It also gives product teams knobs to tune locality vs availability per customer.
